title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
Abstract
FX options are quoted in delta space, not strike space. For each tenor the market gives an at-the-money volatility plus risk reversals and butterflies at fixed delta levels. Turning those five numbers into a continuous, arbitrage-free volatility surface depends on two things that are easy to get wrong. The first is the delta convention, which varies by currency pair and tenor and includes a premium-adjusted variant whose call delta is not monotonic in strike. The second is the butterfly, which is quoted as a market strangle (“broker fly”), not as a direct measure of smile convexity.
This paper documents fxvol, an open-source Python engine implementing Garman–Kohlhagen pricing with a full analytic Greek set, all four FX delta conventions with correct branch selection for premium-adjusted deltas, the Reiswich–Wystup market-strangle calibration at the 25-delta and 10-delta wings, shape-preserving smile interpolation in total variance with a \(C^1\) wing extrapolation, linear-in-total-variance term interpolation, and static no-arbitrage diagnostics based on call convexity, the Durrleman condition, and calendar monotonicity.
The central acceptance criterion is that the calibrated surface must reprice its own inputs. On the illustrative data used throughout, quotes are recovered from the finished surface with a worst error of about \(10^{-11}\) volatility points against a tolerance target of \(0.01\). As a byproduct of the arbitrage diagnostics, the common practice of hard, flat-in-volatility wing extrapolation is shown to create a genuine negative-density butterfly violation at the outermost quoted strikes, and a minimal \(C^1\) smoothing is proposed that removes it.
Keywords: FX options; implied volatility surface; delta conventions; risk reversal; butterfly; market strangle; static arbitrage
JEL: C63, G13, G15

title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
1. Introduction
An FX options desk observes, per tenor, a small set of delta-quoted instruments: the at-the-money (ATM) volatility, the 25-delta and 10-delta risk reversals, and the 25-delta and 10-delta butterflies. Everything else the desk needs — the volatility at an arbitrary strike, the price and Greeks of a vanilla, the implied risk-neutral density, and the inputs to exotic pricing models — has to be built from those quotes. Getting this almost right is easy. Use the wrong delta convention, or treat the butterfly as a convexity number, and the surface still looks reasonable; it is just off by amounts a trading desk would care about.
Malz (1997) gave an early closed-form smile built from the ATM, risk reversal, and strangle quotes. The quoting conventions themselves are documented by Reiswich and Wystup (2010, 2012) and Clark (2011), and the static no-arbitrage conditions in total-variance space come from Gatheral (2006) and Gatheral and Jacquier (2014). What’s harder to find is an open implementation that can be checked end to end. This paper uses one acceptance test above all others: the finished surface must reprice the exact quotes it was built from, to a tolerance far tighter than anything tradeable. The contributions are:

A forward-form Garman–Kohlhagen pricing core with the full analytic Greek set, including vanna and volga, validated against central finite differences.
A complete treatment of the four FX delta conventions (spot or forward, each premium-adjusted or unadjusted), configurable per currency pair and tenor, including a robust strike solver for the premium-adjusted call delta, which is not monotonic in strike and requires explicit selection of the market branch.
An implementation of the Reiswich–Wystup market-strangle butterfly calibration, mapping the quoted butterfly to the scalar price of a single-volatility strangle and solving the smile wing volatilities to reprice that scalar under the risk-reversal constraint.
A smile and term-structure interpolation scheme — monotone cubic in total variance within tenor, linear in total variance across tenors — with a documented \(C^1\) wing extrapolation.
Static no-arbitrage checks (call-price convexity, the Durrleman \(g(k)\) condition, and calendar monotonicity of total variance) that report violations with their location and never silently modify quotes.
An adversarial test suite of 209 tests at roughly 94% line coverage, whose headline test is the round trip above, run for both an unadjusted pair (EURUSD) and a premium-adjusted pair (USDJPY-style).

title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
2. Market Data and Quoting Mechanics
The FX rate \(S\) is quoted as units of domestic (quote) currency per unit of foreign (base) currency; for EURUSD the euro is foreign and the dollar is domestic. Rates are continuously compounded and the forward satisfies covered interest parity, \(F = S\,e^{(r_d - r_f)T}\).
Per tenor the market quotes three instrument types at delta levels of 25 and 10. The risk reversal \(RR = \sigma(\Delta\text{-call}) -
\sigma(\Delta\text{-put})\) measures skew at that delta level. The butterfly \(BF\) measures convexity, but the quoted number is a market-strangle quote: it states that a strangle struck at the two strikes generated by the single volatility \(\sigma_{ATM} + BF\) has a given price — it is not the average of the smile’s wing volatilities minus the ATM volatility, although the two coincide when the risk reversal is zero. The naive relations
\[\sigma(25\Delta c) = \sigma_{ATM} + BF_{25} + RR_{25}/2, \qquad
\sigma(25\Delta p) = \sigma_{ATM} + BF_{25} - RR_{25}/2\]
hold only for the smile strangle and are used only as solver seeds.

title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
3. Methodology

3.1 Pricing model and Greeks
Vanillas are priced with the Garman–Kohlhagen (1983) model in forward form. With forward \(F\), strike \(K\), volatility \(\sigma\), year fraction \(T\), domestic discount factor \(df_d = e^{-r_d T}\), and \(\phi = +1\) for calls, \(-1\) for puts:
\[d_1 = \frac{\ln(F/K) + \sigma^2 T/2}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}\]
\[V = \phi\, df_d \big(F\,N(\phi d_1) - K\,N(\phi d_2)\big)\]
The forward form keeps the delta conventions straight, and put–call parity, \(C - P = df_d(F-K)\), holds exactly by construction. The engine exposes the full analytic Greek set — spot and forward delta, gamma, vega, vanna, volga, theta, and both rhos — each checked against central finite differences at tight tolerance.


3.2 Delta conventions and the premium-adjusted inversion
A quoted 25-delta is ambiguous until two choices are fixed: spot vs. forward delta (market practice uses spot delta up to and including one year, forward delta beyond, cutoff configurable), and premium adjustment — when the premium is paid in the foreign (base) currency, it is itself a position in the underlying and is subtracted from the delta. Whether a pair is premium-adjusted follows from its premium currency: EURUSD is unadjusted, USDJPY is adjusted. The four resulting call deltas are \(N(d_1)\) (unadjusted forward), \(e^{-r_f T}N(d_1)\) (unadjusted spot), \((K/F)N(d_2)\) (premium-adjusted forward), and \(e^{-r_f T}(K/F)N(d_2)\) (premium-adjusted spot); put deltas replace \(N(x)\) with \(-N(-x)\).
For unadjusted conventions the delta-to-strike inversion is closed form. The premium-adjusted call delta needs more care. As a function of strike it rises to an interior maximum and then falls, so one quoted delta can correspond to two strikes. The market convention refers to the higher-strike branch, on which delta is decreasing in strike. The engine locates the turning point exactly by solving \(\sigma\sqrt{T}\,N(d_2) =
n(d_2)\) for \(d_2\) (a single root), then root-finds with Brent’s method only on the branch to the right of that strike. Requests above the attainable maximum raise an error rather than returning a wrong strike. Every convention passes strike-to-delta-to-strike round trips at machine precision, deep wings included.



The premium-adjusted call delta is not monotonic in strike. A target delta near the peak is hit twice; the solver returns the market-branch root (green), not the spurious one (red).




3.3 ATM conventions
The default is the delta-neutral straddle (DNS): the strike at which a straddle has zero net delta in the pair’s own convention. For unadjusted deltas, \(K_{ATM} = F\,e^{+\sigma^2 T/2}\); for premium-adjusted deltas the sign flips, \(K_{ATM} = F\,e^{-\sigma^2 T/2}\), because the straddle delta is proportional to \(N(d_2) - N(-d_2)\) rather than \(N(d_1) - N(-d_1)\). ATM-forward and ATM-spot conventions are also supported.


3.4 Market strangle vs. smile strangle
This is where simple implementations usually go wrong. The quoted butterfly carries exactly one piece of information: the price of the market strangle. Following Reiswich and Wystup (2012), per wing level (25-delta, then 10-delta):

Form the market strangle volatility \(\sigma_{ms} = \sigma_{ATM} + BF\).
Compute the market strangle strikes at delta \(\pm\)level using \(\sigma_{ms}\).
Compute the market strangle price \(v_{ms} = \text{Call}(K_{c,ms}, \sigma_{ms}) + \text{Put}(K_{p,ms}, \sigma_{ms})\).
Solve for smile wing volatilities \((\sigma_c, \sigma_p)\) subject to the risk-reversal constraint \(\sigma_c - \sigma_p = RR\) and the strangle-repricing constraint \(\text{Call}(K_c, \sigma_c) + \text{Put}(K_p, \sigma_p) = v_{ms}\).

The risk-reversal constraint reduces this to a 1-D root find in \(\sigma_c\), solved with Brent’s method, seeded by the naive volatility (exact at zero RR). Convergence and reprice residual are asserted after solving — the calibrator never returns an unverified smile.

The smile-strangle butterfly systematically differs from the quoted market-strangle butterfly whenever the risk reversal is nonzero, and the gap widens with skew — from under a tenth of a basis point at one week to about 2 bp at one year at the 25-delta wing, and about 3.5 bp at the one-year 10-delta wing. A naive construction that plugs the quoted butterfly directly into the smile-strangle algebra is biased at exactly the strikes where exotic hedging happens.


3.5 Smile interpolation and wing extrapolation
The calibration yields five nodes per tenor (10Δ put, 25Δ put, ATM, 25Δ call, 10Δ call) as strike–volatility pairs. Within the quoted range the smile is interpolated with a shape-preserving monotone cubic (PCHIP) in \((k, w)\) coordinates, where \(k = \ln(K/F)\) and \(w = \sigma^2 T\) is total implied variance — PCHIP avoids the overshoot a natural cubic spline exhibits through only five points.
Wing extrapolation is where arbitrage enters. Holding volatility flat beyond the outermost node is continuous but not differentiable there — the slope jumps to zero, a kink that the arbitrage checker flags as a genuine butterfly violation at every 10-delta strike. The production scheme keeps flat volatility as the asymptote but decays the edge slope exponentially over a configurable band (half the node span by default), making the smile \(C^1\) at the last node and keeping the density bounded. The hard-flat mode is still in the library for comparison, and the checker flags it, as it should.



Implied density near the 6M 10-delta call strike. Hard-flat extrapolation (left) produces a negative spike at the last node; the \(C^1\) wing (right) removes it.




3.6 Term-structure interpolation
Across tenors the surface interpolates linearly in total variance at constant forward log-moneyness:
\[w(k, T) = (1-\lambda)\,w_i(k) + \lambda\,w_{i+1}(k), \qquad \lambda = \frac{T - T_i}{T_{i+1} - T_i}\]
with each pillar’s total variance evaluated at \(K_i = F_i e^k\), so moneyness is held constant relative to each pillar’s own forward (Gatheral 2006). Variance is additive in time, keeping calendar arbitrage controllable. Outside the pillar range, volatility is held flat at constant \(k\), so extrapolated total variance grows proportionally with \(T\) and cannot create calendar arbitrage.

title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
4. No-Arbitrage Diagnostics
The engine treats arbitrage checks as diagnostics, never silent repairs. Three static conditions are checked on a dense grid per pillar, with violations reported by tenor, strike, and magnitude:

Undiscounted call prices must be non-increasing and convex in strike (the second derivative is the undiscounted risk-neutral density and must be non-negative).
The Durrleman condition, in total-variance space with derivatives taken in log-moneyness: \[g(k) = \left(1 - \frac{k w'}{2w}\right)^2 - \frac{w'^2}{4}\left(\frac{1}{w} + \frac{1}{4}\right) + \frac{w''}{2} \ge 0\]
Calendar monotonicity: total variance \(w(k,T)\) must be non-decreasing in \(T\) at every fixed \(k\) across adjacent pillars.

Deliberately broken inputs are caught in the test suite: a volatility frown triggers located convexity and Durrleman violations, and a term structure whose short-tenor variance exceeds the next pillar’s triggers located calendar violations. The clean sample surface passes all checks.

title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
6. Software Validation
The engine ships with an adversarial pytest suite of 209 tests, including Hypothesis property-based tests, at roughly 94% line coverage; ruff and mypy both pass clean. Test categories mirror where FX surface implementations actually fail: the headline round-trip test (both unadjusted and premium-adjusted pairs), convention round trips across all four delta conventions with deep wings, a premium-adjusted branch test that constructs a target delta hit by two strikes and asserts the market root is returned, DNS tests including the sign flip, Greeks checked against central finite differences, market-strangle repricing exactness, and deliberately broken surfaces to verify the arbitrage checker actually detects and locates violations.

title: Construction of an Arbitrage-Checked FX Implied Volatility Surface from Delta-Quoted Market Instruments
text:
7. Limitations and Future Work

The tenor calendar uses calendar-day rolls with an act/365 fixed day count and no holiday calendar or cut times; a business-day calendar is an isolated extension point in the data layer.
Arbitrage checks diagnose and locate violations but deliberately do not repair them.
The interpolated smile is a market-consistent interpolant, not a dynamics model; Greeks are sticky-strike by construction.
Two extensions are architected for but not implemented: vanna-volga pricing of exotics (consuming the already-exposed ATM and wing vega, vanna, and volga), and SABR smile calibration (Hagan et al. 2002), implementing the same SmileModel interface the interpolated smile satisfies.

title: Covered Interest Parity Deviations in Emerging Market Currencies
text:
status: in progress

Covered interest parity says that borrowing in one currency, converting it, and hedging the exchange rate with a forward should cost the same as borrowing in the other currency directly. Before 2008 that held almost exactly for the major currencies. Since then it hasn’t, and the gap (the cross-currency basis) has stayed open for years in a way textbook arbitrage says it shouldn’t.
The best-known work on this focuses on G10 pairs. This project looks at emerging-market currencies instead, where capital controls, thinner forward markets, and dollar funding pressure should all matter more.
The data, method, and results will go up here once they’re solid enough to show. Until then, this page is a placeholder for the project.

title: fx-vrp
text:
status: in progress · code: github.com/NavyBlueCheese/fx-vrp

Currency options usually price in more variance than the market ends up delivering. That gap is the variance risk premium (VRP). This project asks two separate questions about it:

Is the premium paid for jump and crash risk, or for ordinary day-to-day (diffusive) risk?
Can anyone actually collect it once delta-hedging happens at discrete intervals and trading costs are realistic?

The second question matters because selling a straddle and delta-hedging it doesn’t earn the raw gap between implied and realised variance. It earns a gamma-weighted version of that gap,
\[\Pi \approx \int_0^T \tfrac12\,\Gamma_u S_u^2\left(\sigma^2_{\text{implied}} - \sigma^2_{\text{realised},u}\right)du,\]
so when the realised variance arrives, relative to where the option’s gamma sits, decides the P&L.
The implied leg comes from CBOE’s EuroCurrency volatility index (EVZ), replicated from option chains with the VIX methodology. The realised leg is built from Dukascopy tick data over the same 30-calendar-day window, with both legs stamped at 16:15 New York so nothing from later in the day leaks into a signal.

title: pairs-trading-backtest
text:
code: github.com/NavyBlueCheese/pairs-trading-backtest

A classic pairs-trading strategy in Python, tested on daily Yahoo Finance data for six stocks in three natural pairs: KO/PEP, XOM/CVX, and JPM/BAC.
Pairs are chosen by cointegration, not correlation. Two stocks can be highly correlated day to day and still drift apart forever; cointegration means some combination of them is stationary, which is what makes betting on the spread coming back reasonable. The test is Engle–Granger: regress one log price on the other, then run an ADF test on the residuals.
Avoiding the usual backtest traps:

The data is split 60/40 by time. Pair selection and the hedge ratio use only the first 60%, and the backtest runs only on the last 40%.
The z-score’s rolling mean and standard deviation (60 days) are lagged one bar, so a day’s spread never appears in its own normalisation.
Signals at the close of day t are filled at the open of t+1.
Costs are 0.1% per leg, 0.4% per round trip.

Trading rules: enter when the z-score passes ±2, exit when it comes back inside ±0.5, stop out beyond ±3.5, and close anything still open after 30 days. The output reports total return, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, and win rate, along with the equity curve and a trade log.

title: tsmom-band
text:
status: paper trading · code: github.com/NavyBlueCheese/tsmom-band

Long-or-flat time-series momentum across four ETFs (SPY, EFA, IEF, GLD), sized for a cash account of about $20 at Interactive Brokers. At that size IBKR’s commission cap of 1% of trade value applies to every order, so a round trip costs 2% of the position. Most of the design is about not giving that money away.
The rules, fixed in a preregistration before any backtest was run:

Signal: the sign of the 21-to-252-day return, per asset. Long or flat, never short.
Sizing: inverse volatility from a 60-day Ledoit–Wolf shrunk covariance, 15% annual volatility target, no leverage.
Rebalance: last trading session of each quarter, 15:45 New York time.
No-trade band: a leg only trades if its target weight differs from the current weight by more than 0.20.
Costs: IBKR Pro’s tiered US-stock schedule, plus SEC and FINRA fees on sells.

None of these get tuned to make a backtest look better. Parameter sweeps are logged as trials and the defaults stay where they are.
The prediction. Before the account was funded, a block bootstrap of the training-period backtest predicted one-year P&L of about +$0.85, with an 80% interval of −$0.26 to +$2.37 and roughly 1.6 trades a year. The point of the project is calibration: does the live result land inside that interval?
How it’s built. Everything runs through an event-driven engine that only ever sees data up to the current bar, so lookahead is impossible by construction. The same strategy code runs in backtest and live. Money amounts use exact decimals, data from 2019 onward is a sealed holdout with a committed hash, and six kill-switch conditions each need a human to clear them.
The paper-trading runner is currently doing its weekly cycles.

title: g10-fx-analysis
text:
code: github.com/NavyBlueCheese/g10-fx-analysis

A statistical look at two years of daily G10 exchange rates against the dollar, pulled live from the Frankfurter API and analysed in R. The notebook asks four questions:

Which currencies move together, and how strongly?
How fat are the return tails compared with a normal distribution?
How stable are risk-adjusted returns over rolling 30-day windows?
Is there volatility clustering, the precondition for GARCH-type models?




Pairwise correlations of daily log returns, ordered by hierarchical clustering.


The clustering pulls out the groups you’d expect. AUD and NZD move almost together (0.89), the European currencies form a block, and JPY is the odd one out, tied mainly to CHF and much more loosely to the commodity currencies.



Absolute daily returns over time with a LOESS trend.


A GitHub Action re-renders the notebook on every push, so the figures in the repository stay current.

I’m Navy, a maths student at Korea University, double majoring in Mathematics and International Commerce. Most of what I work on is quantitative finance, mainly FX: how options on currencies get priced and quoted, how systematic strategies hold up once real trading costs are counted, and where money crossing borders leaves traces in the data. I’m also interested in applied machine learning, in finance and in accessibility. This site collects the papers, write-ups, and code that come out of all that.
Away from the numbers I draw comics and illustrations, do graphic and UX/UI design, and build things for the web.

title: A Statistical Look at the 2024 Thai Senate Ballot-Matching Evidence
text:
What this is (and isn’t)
One argument keeps coming up about the ฮั้ว ส.ว. (Senate collusion) case. Several voters handed in identical ballots, the same names in the same order, but defenders say a chance match isn’t impossible, so collusion can’t be proven statistically. I wanted to see whether that holds up.
This piece doesn’t try to decide the case, say who is guilty, or verify the vote data myself. It does four narrower things:

Re-derives from scratch the probability figures that mathematician Loy Chunpongtong (ลอย ชุนพงษ์ทอง) published about the June 2024 national-level Senate selection, to check the arithmetic.
Checks the method with a Monte Carlo simulation on a small version of the same problem.
Puts the result next to probability thresholds that science, forensics, and the courts already treat as conclusive. That comparison is the actual answer to “it’s technically possible”.
Uses simulated (not real) scores to show why a reported jump in vote totals between 6th and 7th place would point to bloc voting rather than noise.

Figures taken from news reports are linked in the Sources section at the end. Anything I generated myself, like the simulations and the benchmark table, is labelled as mine. Where the public data runs out, I say so.

title: A Statistical Look at the 2024 Thai Senate Ballot-Matching Evidence
text:
1. Background
Thailand chose its Senate (สมาชิกวุฒิสภา) in June 2024 through a closed, multi-round process. Candidates were split into 20 professional groups. At the national round on 26 June, members of each group first voted among themselves in the morning, cutting each group down to 40. In the afternoon, groups voted across for each other’s candidates to pick the final 10 senators per group.
Since then, the Election Commission’s inquiry, the DSI’s AI-assisted video analysis, documents released by opposition MPs, and independent analysts have all pointed at the same accusation: blocs used โพย (cheat-sheets) to coordinate their votes. That would leave a very particular fingerprint, namely ballots with the same names in the same order, filled in by people who say they don’t know each other.
A senator from the accused side has said publicly that nothing unlawful happened because no money changed hands, and that Thai courts have previously ruled that bringing a cheat-sheet into the polling area isn’t a crime in itself. A separate defence, which I’ve seen repeated widely but can’t attribute to any specific senator, goes further: however unlikely an accidental match is, it isn’t impossible, so intent can’t be shown with statistics. That second claim is the one I’m testing.

title: A Statistical Look at the 2024 Thai Senate Ballot-Matching Evidence
text:
2. The probability
The parameters come from public reporting. Each professional group at national level had up to 154 candidates (77 provinces × 2). In the morning round, each voter wrote up to 10 candidate numbers into ten boxes on the ballot. Reports describe 10 ballots carrying the identical sequence. If everyone voted honestly and independently, how likely is that?
A. Two ballots matching. The number of ordered ways to write 10 different names out of 154 is the permutation count \(P(154,10) =
154!/144!\). If voters pick uniformly at random, the chance that a second ballot exactly copies a first one is one over that:
\[\frac{1}{P(154,10)} = \frac{1}{5.567 \times 10^{21}}\]
This is the same “1 in about 5,567 quintillion” figure Loy published. My \(\log_{10}\) of the denominator is 21.746, the same as his to three decimals.
B. All ten ballots matching. Take ballot 1 as the reference. The chance that ballots 2 through 10 each independently match it is that number raised to the ninth power:
\[\frac{1}{P(154,10)^{9}} = \frac{1}{5.134 \times 10^{195}}\]
The denominator has 196 digits. For scale, the observable universe has somewhere around \(10^{82}\) atoms, which is smaller by a factor of about \(10^{114}\).
C. Does the group size matter? Not really. The smallest group reported had 129 candidates, which is the most generous case for the coincidence theory. That gives \(P(129,10) \approx 8.92\times 10^{20}\), so a two-ballot match is still about 1 in \(10^{21}\).
D. How small would the field need to be? Smaller than it can get. Even if there were only 10 candidates, so that every voter had to list all of them, two ballots would only agree on the order 1 time in \(10! = 3{,}628{,}800\). A fifty-fifty chance of a match isn’t reachable with 10 ordered picks at any field size.
E. What if voters aren’t random? This is the fairest objection. Real voters don’t pick uniformly: some candidates are better known, and people from the same province may favour the same names. So suppose, very generously, that every voter in the group ignored everyone except the same 20 favourites and only had to decide the order. Two ballots would still match only once in \(P(20,10) \approx 6.7 \times 10^{11}\) tries, roughly 1 in 670 billion. Popularity can explain why the same names turn up on many ballots. It can’t explain the same names in the same order, ten times over.
In short: two independent ballots matching by chance is about 1 in \(5.6\times10^{21}\), which agrees with Loy’s figure. All ten matching is about 1 in \(5\times10^{195}\).

title: A Statistical Look at the 2024 Thai Senate Ballot-Matching Evidence
text:
3. Checking the method
Numbers this large can’t be checked by brute force, so I tested the formula on a toy version I could simulate: 8 candidates, 3 picks.




value




Theoretical P(match), \(n=8\), \(k=3\)
0.002976


Empirical P(match), 300,000 simulated pairs
0.002787


Relative difference
6.4%



With 300,000 trials the standard error on that estimate is about 3.3%, so the simulated value sits a little under two standard errors from the formula. That’s ordinary sampling noise, and nothing points to the formula being wrong. The same formula applies at \(n=154\), \(k=10\); it just can’t be simulated there, since you’d need well over \(10^{21}\) trials to expect a single match.
Holding \(k=10\) fixed and growing the field shows how fast the odds collapse: about \(10^{-6.6}\) at 10 candidates, \(10^{-11.8}\) at 20, \(10^{-19.8}\) at 100, and \(10^{-21.7}\) at the real figure of 154.



Chance that two independent voters write the same ordered 10-name ballot, by field size.

title: A Statistical Look at the 2024 Thai Senate Ballot-Matching Evidence
text:
4. “It’s not impossible”
The defence is that the match isn’t literally impossible, so it could be coincidence. That’s true, but it doesn’t help. Outside of logical contradictions, nothing in probability is ever exactly impossible. If “not exactly zero” were enough to dismiss evidence, no statistical evidence could count for anything.
Here’s where these numbers sit next to thresholds people already accept:

−9.00

−21.75


Atoms in the observable universe, as a reference (\(10^{82}\))
−82.00


This case: all 10 ballots matching
−195.71



(The DNA and Six Sigma rows are standard order-of-magnitude reference values, not figures from this case. They’re there to show how unlikely something has to be before courts and industry treat chance as ruled out.)
None of those rows is zero either. A drug trial with \(p<0.05\) could still be a fluke under the null hypothesis; we act on it anyway, because calling it chance would be unreasonable. A DNA match at about one in a billion isn’t impossible, and courts still convict on it.
The two-ballot figure is about 13 orders of magnitude rarer than that DNA match. The ten-ballot figure is about 114 orders of magnitude beyond the number of atoms in the universe. And the “not impossible” argument works exactly as well against odds of one in a billion as against odds of one in \(10^{195}\). An argument that never gets weaker however extreme the numbers become isn’t measuring anything. Whether something is possible was never the right question. The right question is whether chance is the best explanation, and here it clearly isn’t.

section: 5. A second pattern: the jump after 6th place

5. A second pattern: the jump after 6th place
Separately from the matching ballots, Loy also pointed to the afternoon round, where candidates ranked 1st to 6th in each group scored unusually high compared with those ranked 7th to 10th. Under independent voting you wouldn’t expect a sharp break like that.

Simulated average vote totals by rank across 200 simulated elections, all 40 finalists shown. Illustrative only.


The gap between 6th and 7th is 0.32 points with independent voting and 7.36 points when a bloc votes together for a slate of six, about 23 times larger. Independent voting gives a smooth slope. A bloc gives a cliff right where its slate ends, because its six candidates all get the same block of extra votes and nobody else does.
That’s the shape Loy described in the real data. This section only shows why that shape would point to coordination if the description is accurate. It doesn’t confirm the real data looks like this or by how much. It’s a test to run once the actual tallies are public.

title: A Statistical Look at the 2024 Thai Senate Ballot-Matching Evidence
text:
6. Summary







Question
Answer




Does the “1 in 5.567 × 10²¹” figure check out?
Yes. Re-derived independently; same number.


Is the method sound?
Yes. A small-scale Monte Carlo agrees within sampling error.


Does the exact group size matter?
No. The smallest reported group (129) still gives about 1 in 10²¹.


Does non-random voting rescue the coincidence theory?
No. Even limiting every voter to the same 20 favourites leaves odds of about 1 in 670 billion per pair.


Does “it’s technically possible” work as a defence?
No. The same logic would throw out DNA evidence, clinical trials, and Six Sigma, none of which deal in zero probabilities either.


Does the reported jump after 6th place matter?
Probably, going by the simulation, but it needs the real vote data to confirm.



Statistics can’t settle intent. Who coordinated with whom, and whether anything was paid or promised, are legal questions these numbers don’t answer. What they do show is that “the match is merely possible, so chance can’t be ruled out” doesn’t survive contact with the standards of evidence used everywhere else.
